Emigrate

EM-uh-grayt -- from Latin e- ('out') + migrare ('to move, migrate'). · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To emigrate move from one's country to another.

Her grandparents chose to emigrate in the 1950s, leaving behind everything they owned for the promise of steadier work.

Worked Example

A family sells their small farm, packs everything they own into three suitcases, and boards a ship, never to live in their home country again.

That permanent departure from one's own country to settle somewhere else is exactly what it means to emigrate.

How Emigrate Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

relocate

relocate: to move to a new place, especially to live

resettle

resettle: to settle again in a new place, especially after leaving another

Antonyms

immigrate

immigrate: to move into a new country to live there permanently

remain

remain: to stay in the same place without leaving

How Strong Is It? — relocate → emigrate → resettle

relocate vs. emigrate

relocate vs. emigrate: Relocate is a broader, more neutral word -- a family can relocate across town or across the ocean, for any reason -- while emigrate specifically means leaving one's own country permanently to live in another.

resettle vs. emigrate

resettle vs. emigrate: Resettle often implies an even more difficult, large-scale transition than emigrate, frequently used for refugees or entire communities rebuilding their lives in a new country after being displaced.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — e-/ex-

prefix — e-/ex-: out (Latin)

root — -migr-

root — -migr-: to move from one place to another (Latin (migrare))

Put it together

Put it together: Emigrate comes from Latin e- ('out') plus migrare ('to move, migrate') -- so to emigrate is literally to 'move out' of one's own country, the mirror image of immigrate, which uses in- ('into') for moving into a new one.

Use the root in a new word: migrate

Use the root in a new word: migrate: Every autumn, thousands of monarch butterflies migrate thousands of miles to warmer winter grounds.

Root Check

Word Choice

Emigrate is very commonly confused with immigrate -- the two describe the same move from opposite points of view. You emigrate FROM your home country, and you immigrate TO your new one; the direction of the prefix (e- 'out' vs. im- 'in') matches the direction of the move.
